claims.text: Coupling machine-learning screening with thermodynamic and kinetic simulations will accelerate identification of strong, ductile, low-density RHEAs.
RHEAs occupy a broad composition space involving refractory elements such as W, Mo, Nb, and Ta.
The starting refractory-alloy search space has no pre-imposed phase constraints.
Candidate RHEAs typically have random solid-solution characteristics.
ML-driven high-throughput screening can predict and narrow candidate RHEA compositions according to strength, ductility, and density trade-offs.
Thermodynamic models and simulation data can inform the ML screening framework.
Room-temperature and elevated-temperature testing can evaluate initial mechanical properties and high-temperature stability, respectively.
Arc melting and homogenization are standard processing routes for the proposed candidates.
The proposed method will stabilize a disordered BCC solid-solution matrix in selected RHEAs.
Lattice distortions in the BCC matrix can be tuned to mediate dislocation movement.
Controlled precipitation can be used to mediate dislocation movement.
ML can correlate descriptors such as atomic-size difference, mixing enthalpy, and configurational entropy with simulated thermodynamic trends.
Composition-dependent atomic-size differences in HEAs cause atoms to deviate from ideal lattice sites.
Lattice distortion provides inherent strengthening in the selected RHEAs.
The integrated method can tailor microstructures to avoid brittle phases.
RHEAs combining refractory elements have demonstrated promising mechanical properties.
RHEAs selected by the integrated method will have a superior combination of ultra-high strength, appreciable ductility, and reduced density compared with trial-and-error-designed alloys.
The method's effectiveness may diminish outside the composition and processing range represented by its training data.
The method's effectiveness depends on the reliability of the underlying simulations.
The magnitude of property improvement and the accuracy of the ML predictions remain uncertain until experimentally validated.
